name: Cercospora leaf spot
summary: A laboratory-confirmed Cannabis leaf-spot disease reported from multiple U.S. field and greenhouse settings. Yellow-green flecks, pale-centered round lesions, dark borders, yellow halos, and central sporulation are compatible but overlap other fungal, bacterial, pest, and abiotic injury. Confirmed Cercospora cf. flagellaris labels require plant-linked fungal morphology, validated multilocus evidence, and preferably pathogenicity evidence; the cf. designation and exact taxonomic resolution cannot be inferred from a photograph.
affectedParts: both leaf surfaces for paired documentation
middle and upper canopy as disease spreads
whole plant for distribution and defoliation context
stages: diagnostic culture and controlled pathogenicity testing
indicators: The reported field sequence begins on older lower-canopy Cannabis leaves rather than being defined by one detached lesion.
Early attached lesions appear as small yellow or yellow-green flecks before the center becomes necrotic.
Developing lesions are commonly round and approximately 2 to 6 mm in the direct hemp reports, with tan, white, or gray centers.
Compatible lesions can develop dark brown to purplish borders and yellow halos, but this color combination is not unique to Cercospora.
Melanized, erumpent conidiophores or conidiophore fascicles arise from lesion centers and may be visible with magnification before the center breaks down.
Microscopy of lesion-linked material can show hyaline, narrow or needle-shaped, septate conidia on compatible conidiophores.
Multiple lesions may coalesce, centers may disintegrate, and affected leaves may become chlorotic or drop as disease advances.

The strongest evidence set links the same plant and lesion to compatible morphology, a single-spored isolate, multilocus placement, symptom reproduction, and recovery from inoculated but not control plants.
exclusions: Dark, round pycnidia embedded in lesions and a compatible Septoria result support the Septoria leaf-spot complex rather than Cercospora.
Gray-brown sooty or velvety sporulation concentrated on the lower leaf surface and Pseudocercospora evidence support olive or sooty leaf spot.
Curvularia, Bipolaris, Alternaria, or another dematiaceous fungus is recovered from representative lesions and supported by appropriate morphology and sequence evidence.
Shot holes, cracked centers, or frog-eye lesions occur without Cercospora-linked structures and Colletotrichum or bacterial evidence better explains the sample.
Angular water-soaked lesions, bacterial streaming or ooze, and a validated bacterial result support bacterial leaf spot or blight.
Purple-gray downy growth on the corresponding lower surface with an oomycete result supports downy mildew.
Superficial white colonies, mite or thrips evidence, chewing injury, or frass explains the visible pattern without lesion-linked Cercospora structures.
A sharp spray, droplet, lamp, aisle, field-edge, or handling boundary with no progressive lesion-linked sporulation supports abiotic or mechanical injury.
Only a detached or low-resolution symptom photograph is available, or one culture is unlinked to the photographed plant and lesion.
Repeated representative samples identify another organism, reveal a mixed-pathogen complex, or fail to produce compatible Cercospora morphology and validated molecular evidence.

progression.description: Small yellow to yellow-green flecks appear on attached older, lower-canopy leaves; this distribution is supportive but not exclusive.
Flecks become round necrotic spots with pale tan, white, or gray centers, darker borders, and sometimes yellow halos.
Melanized conidiophores or fascicles emerge from lesion centers and compatible narrow hyaline conidia can be examined microscopically before centers deteriorate.
Lesions multiply or coalesce, move beyond lower foliage, and can be followed by chlorosis, center loss, or premature defoliation; these endpoints are not specific or inevitable.

The Arkansas/Oklahoma study observed lesions at seven days and all inoculated plants affected at fourteen days after a defined inoculation and 72-hour moist chamber, with controls remaining healthy; those timings are experimental checkpoints, not a universal field clock.

lookAlikes: Pseudocercospora olive or sooty leaf spot
Thrips, spider mite, or hemp russet mite injury
Spray, droplet, light, nutrient, salinity, or water-stress injury
confirmation: Photograph the same attached lesion from upper and lower surfaces with a scale, plus the whole plant and canopy distribution; retain plant, cultivar, location, date, and production-setting identifiers.
Sample multiple actively developing lesions before treatment and keep each lesion linked to its source plant; avoid dry center-only tissue and detached stock imagery.

Use hand-lens and microscopic examination to distinguish melanized erumpent conidiophores and compatible conidia from Septoria pycnidia, Pseudocercospora underside growth, necrotic debris, or residue.
Obtain a lesion-linked single-spored culture and record colony, conidiophore, conidial, and isolate metadata; culture appearance alone does not establish species or causality.

Use validated multilocus evidence when assigning Cercospora cf. flagellaris, preserving loci, accessions, sequence quality, reference set, phylogenetic method, and isolate identity; ITS-only or one BLAST match remains provisional.

When causal confirmation is required, prefer symptom reproduction on Cannabis, recovery of the same organism, and symptomless matched controls; detection from one lesion does not prove every field spot shares that cause.

Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, upper-surface-only, culture-unlinked, ITS-only, single-locus-only, mixed-pathogen, low-resolution, stock, vendor, forum, generated, and rights-unclear samples out of the confirmed class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Photograph whole-plant distribution and paired leaf surfaces before removing tissue, then preserve several untreated actively developing lesions for diagnosis.
Separate symptomatic propagation material from clean stock and limit movement of wet leaves, tools, or debris while organism identity is unresolved.
Map cultivar blocks, canopy levels, irrigation, leaf wetness, airflow, residue, weeds, field edges, and exposure boundaries so mixed disease and abiotic patterns are not collapsed into one label.
correctivePlan: Base sanitation and any locally permitted disease-management response on the organism confirmed by a diagnostic laboratory rather than a symptom chart.
Remove or contain confirmed diseased material and residue as appropriate to the production system, then track marked plants and new foliage for incident lesions.
Evaluate intervention with new lesion incidence, severity, and laboratory follow-up; old necrotic tissue and treatment response do not retrospectively confirm species identity.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and avoid moving symptomatic plants, tools, or debris into clean areas.
Improve air circulation, minimize avoidable leaf wetness, and manage infected crop or weed residue where feasible and locally appropriate.
Scout consistent plant IDs across both leaf surfaces and canopy levels over time so early lesions, sporulation, spread, and confounders remain linked.
warnings: Human review is mandatory for symptom-only, detached, upper-surface-only, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, ITS-only, single-locus-only, low-resolution, generated, stock, or rights-unclear samples.
Round pale-centered lesions, dark borders, yellow halos, chlorosis, center loss, defoliation, and lower-canopy onset are not unique to Cercospora.
The cf. flagellaris designation is laboratory-bounded and cannot be resolved from lesion color, lesion dimensions, central dark structures, one culture, or ordinary image and video evidence.

The two-to-six-millimeter lesion range, Florida foliage involvement, Kentucky canopy patterns, and seven- or fourteen-day controlled results are study-specific observations, not universal timing, severity, cultivar, yield, or action thresholds.
Cercospora, Bipolaris, and Septoria occurred together in Kentucky field experiments; a combined leaf-spot severity or yield result cannot be assigned to Cercospora alone.
No image or video was added because available article and institutional figures lacked sufficiently clear item-level automated-training permission and panel-resolved labels.
A positive organism result from one sampled lesion does not establish that every lesion on a plant or in a field has the same cause.

sources.title: First Report of Cercospora cf. flagellaris on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Cercospora leaf spot began on older lower-canopy hemp leaves as small yellow flecks and progressed to round 2 to 6 mm lesions with tan-to-white centers, dark brown-to-purplish borders, and yellow halos.
Melanized conidiophores could become visible in lesion centers before centers disintegrated.
Whole-plant inoculation reproduced similar symptoms and the fungus was recovered again, supporting pathogenicity rather than visual association alone.
The Kentucky observations and lesion dimensions are report-specific and do not establish a universal onset date, canopy position, lesion size, or severity threshold.

sources.title: First Report of Cercospora Leaf Spot Caused by Cercospora cf. flagellaris on Industrial Hemp in Florida
supportedClaims: A 2019 Florida greenhouse and field report described small yellow flecks on older leaves progressing through the canopy to pale tan or white, yellow-haloed lesions with central conidiophore fascicles.
Severe disease in the reported plants included chlorosis and premature defoliation, but the observed incidence and foliage involvement are trial-specific rather than universal severity thresholds.
Three single-spored isolates were identified using morphology plus ITS and actin sequences, and pathogenicity testing reproduced symptoms and recovered the organism from inoculated plants.

The report explicitly identified epidemiology, cultivar response, fungicide sensitivity, and management as evidence gaps; its observations do not validate visual-only cultivar susceptibility or treatment rules.

sources.title: First Report of Cercospora Leaf Spot Caused by Cercospora cf. flagellaris on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Arkansas and Oklahoma
supportedClaims: Field lesions in Arkansas and Oklahoma began on older lower-canopy hemp leaves as yellow-green specks and developed into round 2 to 4 mm necrotic lesions with white, tan, or gray centers and brown borders.
Five single-spored isolates produced melanized erumpent conidiophores and hyaline, needle-shaped conidia and were evaluated with ITS, tef1, histone H3, calmodulin, and actin sequence evidence.

A multilocus phylogeny grouped all five isolates with Cercospora cf. flagellaris, while the cf. designation still communicates bounded taxonomic resolution rather than an image-resolvable species label.
Whole-plant inoculations of Sour Space Candy and Red Kross reproduced lesions, left water-treated controls healthy, and yielded the same organism; the experiment was repeated with the same result.

Seven- and fourteen-day symptom observations followed a defined spore concentration, 72-hour moist chamber, growth-chamber regime, two cultivars, and four plants per treatment and are not universal field timelines.

sources.title: Leaf Spot Disease Development and Its Effect on Yield of Essential Oil-Producing Hemp Cultivars in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Two Kentucky field experiments in 2020 and 2021 evaluated Bipolaris, Cercospora, and Septoria leaf spots across four essential-oil hemp cultivar groups.
In those experiments Bipolaris was first observed seven to eight weeks after planting and increased through the end of the season; this is a study observation, not a universal onset rule.
All three evaluated leaf spots were more severe in the middle canopy than the upper canopy, and susceptibility differed among cultivar groups; neither pattern is a universal diagnostic threshold.
Reported yield associations concerned the combined leaf-spot disease complex under the tested cultivars, sites, and seasons and must not be attributed to Bipolaris alone.
Overlapping leaf-spot syndromes mean paired canopy observations, temporal follow-up, fungal morphology, culture, and molecular diagnostics are more reliable than one lesion photograph.
